definition: Access Control rules (ACLs) control whether a user can access a platform object or perform an operation such as read, write, create, delete, or execute.
whatItDoes: ACLs protect record data, field data, and other platform resources by evaluating required roles, conditions, and scripts before access is granted.
keyComponents: Type, operation, and name determine what resource the ACL protects.
ACL evaluation can include required roles, a condition builder, and an advanced script.
Record and field access must both evaluate correctly when field security is involved.
Specific rules are evaluated before more generic parent-table or wildcard matches.
realTimeExamples: Restrict write access to Incident work_notes so only support staff can update it.
Protect a Script Include or UI Page with execute access so only the right role can invoke it.
interviewPitfalls: Explaining ACLs as only role checks and ignoring conditions and scripts.
Testing only one user path instead of validating both allowed and denied outcomes.
Putting expensive GlideRecord logic in ACL scripts without considering performance.

definition: Business Rules are server-side scripts that run when records are queried, inserted, updated, deleted, or displayed.
whatItDoes: They enforce business logic around database operations, maintain data integrity, trigger follow-on processing, and prepare data for the client when needed.
keyComponents: The table defines which record set the rule runs against.
The When setting controls timing such as before, after, async, display, or query.
Conditions narrow when the rule runs and reduce unnecessary execution.
Advanced scripts commonly use current and previous objects plus server-side APIs like GlideRecord and GlideSystem.
realTimeExamples: Set default values or validate required data before an Incident is inserted.
Create a follow-on task or queue an event after a Change request is updated.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing Business Rules with client-side behavior on the form.
Using a Business Rule without a condition when the logic only applies to a subset of records.
Causing recursion by updating the same record repeatedly without safeguards.

definition: A before Business Rule runs before the database operation is committed.
whatItDoes: It is typically used to validate data or set field values on the current record before insert, update, or delete processing completes.
keyComponents: Runs in the transaction before the row is committed.
Can change values on current without requiring a separate update() call.
Best used for validation, normalization, and defaulting logic.
realTimeExamples: Set priority from impact and urgency before an Incident is saved.
Prevent invalid state changes when mandatory supporting data is missing.
interviewPitfalls: Calling current.update() inside a before rule and creating recursion risk.
Using a before rule for work that should happen after the save, like noncritical follow-on processing.

definition: An after Business Rule runs immediately after the database operation completes on the current record.
whatItDoes: It is typically used when the current record is already saved and related processing should happen next, such as updating dependent records or generating follow-on actions.
keyComponents: Runs after the current record operation completes.
Useful for logic that depends on the saved state of the record.
Often used for related-record updates, notifications, or event generation.
realTimeExamples: Create or update related task records after a parent request changes state.
Queue an event for downstream notification processing after a record update.
interviewPitfalls: Using after rules for simple field defaulting that should be handled in a before rule.
Putting heavy processing in an after rule when async is more appropriate.

definition: An async Business Rule runs after the database transaction commits, but the logic is deferred to background processing.
whatItDoes: It offloads noninteractive server work so the user does not wait for long-running post-save logic.
keyComponents: Runs after commit instead of blocking the user transaction.
Best for noncritical follow-on work such as integrations or heavier calculations.
Cannot be used when immediate client-visible results are required.
realTimeExamples: Push a saved record to an external system after commit.
Run nonurgent enrichment or downstream processing after an update.
interviewPitfalls: Expecting async logic to finish before the user sees the saved record.
Using async when downstream logic must happen synchronously for data correctness.

definition: A display Business Rule runs when a form is being prepared for display and is commonly used to populate g_scratchpad values for the client.
whatItDoes: It sends server-derived information to the client before the form renders so client scripts can use it without extra round trips.
keyComponents: Runs during record display rather than on save.
Often populates g_scratchpad for client-side consumption.
Useful when the client needs server-only data at form load time.
realTimeExamples: Populate a scratchpad flag so client logic knows whether the current user can see a custom action.
Send related-record summary data needed by an onLoad client script.
interviewPitfalls: Using a display rule for database update logic.
Sending too much data to g_scratchpad instead of only what the client needs.

definition: A query Business Rule runs before a database query executes and can change the query conditions that are applied.
whatItDoes: It restricts or modifies which records are returned from a query, often as an additional security or visibility control.
keyComponents: Runs on query operations rather than insert or update.
Can add query conditions to current before records are returned.
Should be used carefully because it affects all matching queries on the table.
realTimeExamples: Filter a custom table so users only see records for their assignment group.
Apply a global visibility filter to archived or restricted records.
interviewPitfalls: Using a query Business Rule where ACLs should be the primary security mechanism.
Adding complex logic that unexpectedly hides records across the platform.

definition: In Business Rules, current represents the active record being processed and previous represents the record values before the operation when that context is available.
whatItDoes: These objects let scripts compare old and new values, detect field changes, and act on the record in context.
keyComponents: current is a GlideRecord-like object for the record in flight.
previous is used to compare prior values in synchronous Business Rule contexts.
Methods such as changes() and changesTo() are often used for field-change detection.
realTimeExamples: Trigger logic only when priority changes from 3 to 1.
Add work notes only when assignment group changes.
interviewPitfalls: Assuming previous is always available in every execution context.
Comparing string values manually when field change helper methods are available.

definition: Client Scripts are client-side JavaScript that run on forms when they load, change, or submit.
whatItDoes: They control form behavior such as validating data, changing field states, showing messages, and reacting to user input before the request reaches the server.
keyComponents: Client Script types include onLoad, onChange, and onSubmit for forms.
They commonly use client APIs like g_form and GlideAjax.
They should focus on form behavior, not server-side database operations.
realTimeExamples: Make a field mandatory when another field changes to a specific value.
Warn users before submitting a high-priority request without required details.
interviewPitfalls: Trying to use server-side APIs like GlideRecord directly in client scripts.
Putting too much logic in onLoad scripts and slowing the form down.

definition: An onLoad Client Script runs when a form loads before the user interacts with it.
whatItDoes: It initializes form state, messages, or field behavior based on the data already on the form.
keyComponents: Runs during form load.
Uses g_form for field visibility, mandatory state, messages, and related client actions.
Should be used sparingly because it affects form load time.
realTimeExamples: Display a warning banner when an Incident is already in a critical state.
Hide or show a section based on the current record values.
interviewPitfalls: Adding heavy logic that delays the form becoming interactive.
Using onLoad for validation that belongs in onSubmit.

definition: An onChange Client Script runs when a specific field value changes on a form.
whatItDoes: It reacts to user input in real time and can modify other fields, show messages, or request server data when needed.
keyComponents: Receives control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading, and isTemplate parameters.
Typically targets one field and responds to value changes.
Often combines g_form with GlideAjax when server data is required.
realTimeExamples: When state changes to Closed Complete, make resolution fields mandatory.
When Requested for changes, retrieve related server data such as manager or email.
interviewPitfalls: Ignoring isLoading and firing logic during form initialization.
Creating field-update loops by changing the same field repeatedly.

definition: An onSubmit Client Script runs when the user submits a form.
whatItDoes: It validates the final state of the form before the data is sent to the server and can block submission by returning false.
keyComponents: Runs at submit time rather than during field edits.
Best for final validation checks and user confirmations.
Can prevent submission when the form is incomplete or invalid.
realTimeExamples: Prevent save when a priority-1 ticket is missing a business impact explanation.
Ask the user to confirm a destructive or high-risk action before submit.
interviewPitfalls: Doing work in onSubmit that should have been handled earlier in onChange.
Assuming client-side validation alone is enough for critical server-side data rules.

definition: UI Policies are client-side rules that control form and field behavior, often without requiring custom script.
whatItDoes: They make fields mandatory, read-only, or visible based on conditions and can optionally run UI Policy Scripts for extra client logic.
keyComponents: UI Policy conditions determine when the policy applies.
UI Policy Actions set field mandatory, visible, or read-only states.
UI Policy scripts extend the behavior when declarative actions are not enough.
realTimeExamples: Make Closure code mandatory only when state changes to Closed.
Show additional justification fields when a sensitive category is selected.
interviewPitfalls: Using a client script when a simpler UI Policy would do the job.
Forgetting that UI Policies affect forms, not direct server-side imports or integrations.

definition: Data Policies enforce field rules such as mandatory or read-only requirements at the data layer, beyond form-only behavior.
whatItDoes: They help ensure consistent data quality across form submissions and, when configured, other data entry paths such as imports or web services.
keyComponents: A Data Policy has conditions that determine when it applies.
Data Policy Rules define the affected fields and required behavior.
Data Policies complement UI Policies by enforcing rules beyond the visible form experience.
realTimeExamples: Require a business owner field whenever a custom service record is marked active.
Enforce mandatory fields on records loaded from noninteractive sources.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing Data Policies with UI Policies and assuming they behave the same way.
Not checking whether the policy is configured to enforce requirements for non-form updates.

definition: Script Includes are reusable server-side script logic that define functions or classes and run only when explicitly called.
whatItDoes: They centralize shared logic so Business Rules, APIs, background scripts, and other server-side components can reuse it consistently.
keyComponents: Script Includes can be classless on-demand functions or class-based definitions.
Accessible from and application scope settings affect how they can be called.
Client-callable Script Includes are a special case used with GlideAjax.
realTimeExamples: Create a utility class that calculates SLA targets or assignment logic used by multiple scripts.
Centralize integration payload-building logic so several Business Rules can reuse it.
interviewPitfalls: Duplicating complex logic in multiple Business Rules instead of reusing a Script Include.
Ignoring scope and accessibility settings when calling a Script Include across applications.

definition: A client-callable Script Include is a Script Include that can be invoked from client-side scripts, typically through GlideAjax.
whatItDoes: It exposes controlled server-side logic to the client so forms can request server data without loading full records unnecessarily.
keyComponents: The Script Include must be marked client callable.
In scoped apps, GlideAjax patterns commonly extend global.AbstractAjaxProcessor.
Methods return targeted data instead of exposing unrestricted database access.
realTimeExamples: Return a user's email or manager information when the Requested for field changes.
Validate a value against server-side rules from a form without submitting the record.
interviewPitfalls: Marking a Script Include client callable but not designing safe, narrow methods.
Returning more data than necessary instead of a minimal response.

definition: GlideAjax is a client-to-server mechanism that lets client scripts call a server-side Script Include and receive a response asynchronously.
whatItDoes: It fetches server data or performs controlled server-side checks without requiring a full form submission.
keyComponents: Client scripts send parameters to a client-callable Script Include.
The server-side logic returns XML or JSON-based data for the client to parse.
Using GlideAjax can be more efficient than returning an entire referenced record.
realTimeExamples: Retrieve a Requested for user's email instead of loading the full user record client side.
Check a server-side rule during form entry and update the UI based on the response.
interviewPitfalls: Using GlideAjax for logic that could be satisfied from data already on the form.
Building wide, generic server calls instead of focused methods with small responses.

definition: GlideRecord is the primary server-side API for querying, inserting, updating, and deleting records in ServiceNow tables.
whatItDoes: It interacts directly with table data and is used throughout server-side scripting for CRUD operations and record traversal.
keyComponents: Common methods include addQuery(), addEncodedQuery(), query(), next(), initialize(), insert(), update(), and deleteRecord().
It operates against a target table and exposes that table's fields on the record object.
Efficient query design matters for performance and data safety.
realTimeExamples: Find active incidents assigned to a group and update related fields.
Create a related task record after a parent request meets a condition.
interviewPitfalls: Querying large tables without adequate filters or limits.
Using GlideRecord on the client instead of server-side only patterns.

definition: GlideAggregate is a server-side API built for aggregate operations such as COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX, and AVG on table data.
whatItDoes: It performs grouped or aggregated queries more efficiently than looping through raw GlideRecord result sets for reporting-style calculations.
keyComponents: Supports aggregate methods like COUNT and SUM.
Can group results using orderBy()/grouping patterns depending on the use case.
Optimized for aggregate use cases compared with manual counting loops.
realTimeExamples: Count incidents by category over a time window.
Calculate aggregate request volume for a dashboard or summary job.
interviewPitfalls: Using GlideRecord loops to count records when GlideAggregate is more appropriate.
Forgetting that aggregate results must be read with aggregate-specific methods.

definition: The gs object exposes the GlideSystem API, a core server-side utility API for logging, messaging, user context, dates, and event-related operations.
whatItDoes: It provides platform utility functions rather than direct database CRUD behavior.
keyComponents: Common uses include logging, getting current user information, adding messages, and generating events.
It is available in server-side contexts such as Business Rules, Script Includes, and background scripts.
It complements record APIs like GlideRecord rather than replacing them.
realTimeExamples: Write debug or error information to logs while troubleshooting a script.
Queue an event or add an info message after server-side processing.
interviewPitfalls: Treating GlideSystem like a database API.
Overusing log statements in production logic without a debugging strategy.

definition: An encoded query is a compact query string format used by ServiceNow to represent filters that GlideRecord and related APIs can execute.
whatItDoes: It lets scripts reuse list-style filter logic in a single string rather than chaining many query conditions.
tablesInvolved: Target table varies by use case
keyComponents: Encoded queries often originate from list filters or condition builders.
They can be passed to addEncodedQuery() for server-side filtering.
They are powerful but should still be readable and maintainable.
realTimeExamples: Reuse a saved Incident filter in a background script.
Apply a complex date-and-state filter in a Script Include with a single query string.
interviewPitfalls: Copying opaque encoded queries into code without documenting intent.
Using encoded queries where a few explicit conditions would be clearer.

definition: Import Sets provide a staged data-import mechanism for bringing external data into ServiceNow before transforming it into target tables.
whatItDoes: They load source data into staging tables, then rely on transform maps and field maps to create or update target records.
keyComponents: Data is loaded into a staging table first, not directly into the target table.
Transform Maps move data from staging to target tables.
Import quality depends on field mapping, coalesce, and error review.
realTimeExamples: Load a spreadsheet of users or assets into a staging table before transforming the data.
Import CI data from an external export and review row errors before promoting records.
interviewPitfalls: Treating the staging table as the final data model.
Ignoring transform history and row errors after a nominally successful run.

definition: A Data Source defines where import data comes from and how it is loaded into a staging table.
whatItDoes: It identifies the external source format or location and provides the configuration used by Load Data and import operations.
keyComponents: A Data Source defines the incoming file or connection details.
Loading a data source populates a staging table used by the import process.
Different source types can require different configuration options.
realTimeExamples: Configure a CSV Data Source for user onboarding imports.
Use a spreadsheet Data Source to stage historical asset records.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing a Data Source with the Transform Map that moves data to the target table.
Ignoring file format and encoding issues that affect load quality.

definition: A Transform Map defines how data from an import staging table maps into a target table.
whatItDoes: It controls the field mappings, transform behavior, and options such as whether business rules or mandatory enforcement run during the transformation.
keyComponents: Source table and target table are the core transform map relationship.
Field Maps connect incoming columns to target fields.
Options like Run business rules, Enforce mandatory fields, and Copy empty values affect import behavior.
realTimeExamples: Map staged employee IDs and names into the user table.
Control whether an import updates existing records or inserts new ones.
interviewPitfalls: Assuming a successful transform means the data is correct.
Ignoring how transform-map options change downstream behavior and performance.

definition: Transform Scripts are server-side scripts that run at specific points during a transformation to control or enrich import behavior.
whatItDoes: They let you manipulate source and target data, handle exceptions, or add custom logic during import processing.
keyComponents: Transform Scripts run in event stages such as onBefore or onAfter depending on the script type.
They use source and target objects provided by the transform runtime.
They should be used when field maps alone are not enough.
realTimeExamples: Normalize an incoming source value before writing it to the target table.
Skip or reroute certain import rows when custom business conditions are met.
interviewPitfalls: Using transform scripts for logic that should be solved with clean field mapping.
Adding opaque import logic without documenting which transform stage it belongs to.

definition: Coalesce is a field-map option used during transforms to decide whether an incoming row should update an existing target record or create a new one.
whatItDoes: It matches staged rows to target rows based on one or more fields so imports can update existing records instead of always inserting duplicates.
keyComponents: Coalesce can be defined on one or multiple target fields.
If a matching target record is found, the record is updated.
If no match is found, a new record is inserted.
realTimeExamples: Use employee number to update an existing user instead of creating a duplicate.
Use serial number to match hardware assets during an import.
interviewPitfalls: Choosing nonunique coalesce fields and updating the wrong record.
Assuming no coalesce means partial updates rather than guaranteed inserts.

definition: Field Maps define how individual source columns map to target fields within a Transform Map.
whatItDoes: They align source data to the correct target schema and can participate in behaviors such as coalescing.
keyComponents: Each field map pairs a source field with a target field.
Coalesce can be configured at the field-map level.
Field maps can be created automatically or manually refined.
realTimeExamples: Map a spreadsheet column named Employee ID to user.employee_number.
Map a source serial number column to a hardware asset serial number field and mark it as coalesce.
interviewPitfalls: Relying on automap without validating that names and types actually align.
Forgetting that a bad field map can silently distort imported data.

definition: Notifications are configured rules that send outbound messages such as emails when specific events or record conditions occur.
whatItDoes: They automate communication to users or groups based on platform activity and event processing.
keyComponents: Notifications define recipients, content, and send conditions.
They can be triggered by events or record conditions.
The actual outbound email records can be tracked separately.
realTimeExamples: Send an approval email when a request enters an approval state.
Notify an assignment group when a major incident is created.
interviewPitfalls: Creating overlapping notifications that send duplicate emails.
Confusing the event that triggers a notification with the notification record itself.

definition: Events are queued platform signals used to trigger downstream processing such as notifications or script actions.
whatItDoes: They decouple the business action from the follow-on handler so downstream logic can react consistently.
keyComponents: An event has a name and usually references a record context.
Events are commonly generated from server-side code using gs.eventQueue().
Notifications and Script Actions can listen for specific event names.
realTimeExamples: Queue a custom event after a request is approved.
Generate an event when a key field changes so notifications react consistently.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing events with notifications themselves.
Queuing events without a clear downstream consumer.

definition: gs.eventQueue() is a GlideSystem method that queues an event for later processing.
whatItDoes: It places an event on the platform event queue so notifications or script actions can process it asynchronously.
keyComponents: Called from server-side scripts.
Typically includes an event name, record context, and optional parameters.
Supports event-driven design instead of hardwiring notification logic into every script.
realTimeExamples: Queue an event when a change request moves to an approved state.
Trigger a custom notification flow using event parameters for extra context.
interviewPitfalls: Using gs.eventQueue without defining who consumes the event.
Putting all notification logic in Business Rules instead of event-driven handlers.

definition: Assignment Rules automatically determine the user or group that should receive work based on record conditions.
whatItDoes: They standardize routing logic so records are assigned consistently without manual triage every time.
keyComponents: Rules are evaluated against record conditions.
They can assign to a group, user, or both depending on configuration.
They are commonly used on task-based processes such as Incident or Case routing.
realTimeExamples: Route network incidents to the network support group based on category.
Assign onboarding requests to a regional fulfillment team.
interviewPitfalls: Overlapping rules that compete and create unexpected assignments.
Treating assignment logic as ad hoc script logic instead of a maintainable routing design.

definition: Approvals represent records and logic used to request and track acceptance decisions before work can continue.
whatItDoes: They pause or gate a process until approvers accept, reject, or otherwise decide on the work.
keyComponents: Approval records track the approver, state, and parent record relationship.
Approval generation can be driven by workflow, flow, or platform logic.
Downstream process steps often depend on approval state changes.
realTimeExamples: Require manager approval before a catalog request continues to fulfillment.
Pause a change process until CAB or technical approval is completed.
interviewPitfalls: Explaining approvals only as emails instead of records and process gates.
Ignoring what happens when approvals are reassigned, canceled, or become stale.

definition: A Catalog Item is an orderable good or service in the Service Catalog.
whatItDoes: It collects request information from users and drives request, requested item, task, approval, and fulfillment processing.
keyComponents: Catalog Items define the orderable offering itself.
Variables collect user inputs.
Downstream fulfillment typically creates request and requested item records.
realTimeExamples: Order a laptop, software, or access package through a standard request form.
Submit a new service request that triggers approvals and fulfillment tasks.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing a Catalog Item with a Record Producer or Order Guide.
Ignoring the request data model created after submission.

definition: A Record Producer is a catalog construct that creates a target record directly, often instead of creating a standard requested item flow.
whatItDoes: It lets users submit catalog-style forms that generate records such as incidents, HR cases, or custom table records.
keyComponents: It is configured as a Service Catalog item type.
Variables capture input and map into the target record.
The target record is created directly on the configured table.
realTimeExamples: Create an Incident from a simplified help form in the catalog.
Create a custom onboarding record directly from a producer form.
interviewPitfalls: Describing a Record Producer as the same thing as a standard Catalog Item request.
Ignoring variable-to-target-field mapping behavior.

definition: A Variable Set is a reusable group of catalog variables that can be attached to multiple catalog items or order guides.
whatItDoes: It reduces duplication by letting multiple catalog experiences share the same grouped question set.
keyComponents: Variable Sets can be attached to multiple catalog items or order guides.
They help standardize repeated question groups.
Catalog scripts and policies should reference internal names correctly.
realTimeExamples: Reuse employee contact variables across several onboarding catalog items.
Attach the same access-justification variables to multiple access request items.
interviewPitfalls: Duplicating the same variables across many items instead of using a set.
Using names or labels inconsistently when client logic should target internal names.

definition: An Order Guide is a catalog construct that helps users request multiple related catalog items in one guided experience.
whatItDoes: It collects high-level inputs and can cascade variables to included items so a bundle of requests is created together.
keyComponents: Order Guides group multiple catalog items.
Guide variables help determine which included items and values are used.
Variable cascading can pass shared answers to generated items.
realTimeExamples: Request a new employee bundle that includes laptop, software, and access items.
Use guide variables to drive which included requests are created.
interviewPitfalls: Describing an Order Guide as just a larger single Catalog Item.
Ignoring variable cascading and included-item behavior.

definition: Requested Item Flow refers to the backend request lifecycle after a catalog item is ordered, especially how the requested item moves through fulfillment.
whatItDoes: It connects the request, requested item, approvals, and catalog tasks that fulfill the order.
keyComponents: The request record is the umbrella container.
The requested item tracks item-specific fulfillment state.
Catalog tasks and approvals drive the execution of fulfillment work.
realTimeExamples: A laptop order creates a request, one requested item, approval records, and catalog tasks for procurement and imaging.
A software request moves the requested item through approval and then automated fulfillment.
interviewPitfalls: Confusing the request, requested item, and catalog task tables.
Explaining fulfillment without referencing the actual request data model.

definition: A MID Server is a Java application installed inside the customer network that provides a secure bridge between the ServiceNow instance and external systems or internal infrastructure.
whatItDoes: It enables Discovery, integrations, orchestration, and other outbound interactions without exposing the instance directly to internal endpoints.
keyComponents: The MID Server runs inside the network and communicates outbound to the instance.
It commonly supports Discovery, Service Mapping, integrations, and automation workloads.
Work is exchanged through the ECC Queue.
realTimeExamples: Use a MID Server to discover servers behind a firewall.
Route internal integration traffic through a MID Server for secure connectivity.
interviewPitfalls: Describing the MID Server as if it stores primary business data.
Ignoring network placement, credentials, and capability considerations.

definition: The ECC Queue is the communication point between the ServiceNow instance and MID Server-driven work.
whatItDoes: It stores output work items for MID Servers and input/result messages returned from MID Server processing.
keyComponents: The queue contains both outbound work and inbound results.
Agent, topic, payload, queue direction, and state are key troubleshooting fields.
Discovery and MID-based integrations rely heavily on ECC Queue records.
realTimeExamples: Review ECC Queue records when a probe or pattern does not complete as expected.
Check the payload and error string to understand a failed MID-executed command.
interviewPitfalls: Looking only at Discovery Status and not tracing the underlying ECC messages.
Treating an ECC completion code as proof that the target data is correct without deeper inspection.

definition: A Discovery Schedule defines when and where ServiceNow Discovery runs against a set of IP ranges, CIs, or cloud targets.
whatItDoes: It controls discovery execution timing, target scope, and the generation of status records and ECC activity for the run.
keyComponents: The schedule defines targets and runtime timing.
Discovery runs produce status records you can inspect.
Related ECC Queue activity shows the actual work sent through MID processing.
realTimeExamples: Run nightly server discovery against a data-center subnet.
Review discovery status and related ECC activity when a schedule fails to populate expected CIs.
interviewPitfalls: Blaming schedules for every Discovery issue when credentials, MID placement, or probes are the actual problem.
Explaining Discovery only at the schedule level without mentioning status and ECC traces.

definition: The Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE) is the CMDB framework that identifies CIs uniquely and reconciles updates from authorized data sources.
whatItDoes: It helps prevent duplicate CIs, applies identification logic, and enforces source authority rules when CI data is inserted or updated.
keyComponents: IRE uses identification rules to find the correct CI.
It uses reconciliation rules to decide which sources can update which attributes.
It supports APIs and payload-based create or update processing for CMDB data.
realTimeExamples: Process imported or discovered CI payloads through IRE instead of writing directly to CMDB tables.
Use IRE to prevent duplicate server records when multiple discovery or integration sources send data.
interviewPitfalls: Explaining IRE only as deduplication and skipping reconciliation behavior.
Updating CMDB records directly when IRE should be the controlled entry point.

definition: Identification Rules define the attributes or identifiers that IRE uses to determine whether an incoming CI payload matches an existing CI.
whatItDoes: They establish CI matching logic so records can be identified consistently across sources.
keyComponents: Rules are defined per class and can be inherited through the CMDB hierarchy.
They use one or more identifier entries and attributes for matching.
Strong identification logic is essential to prevent duplicate CIs.
realTimeExamples: Identify a server by serial number or another reliable combination of attributes.
Tune a class rule when integration payloads are not matching the intended CI.
interviewPitfalls: Choosing weak identifiers that are not truly stable or unique.
Ignoring class inheritance when troubleshooting why a rule is applied.

definition: Reconciliation Rules define which data source is authoritative for updating CI attributes when multiple sources send data to the CMDB.
whatItDoes: They prevent lower-authority sources from overwriting trusted attribute values on CIs.
keyComponents: Rules are applied during IRE-driven update scenarios.
They determine source authority for attribute updates.
They help maintain CMDB trust when Discovery, integrations, and imports all contribute data.
realTimeExamples: Allow Discovery to update operational server attributes while another source owns financial attributes.
Prevent a low-trust import from overwriting a value already owned by a higher-authority source.
interviewPitfalls: Talking about reconciliation only as record matching instead of attribute-authority control.
Ignoring source precedence when CMDB values appear to revert unexpectedly.

definition: CMDB tables store Configuration Items in a class hierarchy rooted in the CMDB data model.
whatItDoes: They organize CI records by class so applications can store common and class-specific attributes correctly.
keyComponents: cmdb_ci is the base for CI class extension.
Child class tables inherit from parent CMDB classes.
Choosing the correct class matters for relationships, patterns, and downstream behavior.
realTimeExamples: Store a server in the right CI class so Discovery and Service Mapping work correctly.
Model different infrastructure types with inherited CMDB classes rather than one flat custom table.
interviewPitfalls: Treating CMDB as one generic table instead of a class hierarchy.
Using the wrong class and losing expected identification, reconciliation, or relationship behavior.

definition: CI Relationships represent dependencies or associations between Configuration Items in the CMDB.
whatItDoes: They help model how infrastructure and services connect so impact analysis, Service Mapping, and operational views are meaningful.
keyComponents: Relationship records connect parent and child CIs using a relationship type.
The relationship type defines the semantic meaning of the connection.
Relationship quality directly affects impact and topology outcomes.
realTimeExamples: Model an application server running on a virtual machine that depends on an infrastructure service.
Use CI relationships to understand downstream impact when a shared database fails.
interviewPitfalls: Creating relationships without a clear semantic meaning or type.
Ignoring relationship accuracy when troubleshooting impact or service maps.
